Only the harness's own documented CLI touches the registration and no copy is uninstalled, and because no declaration of the name is left on the old tag, no stale registration at another scope can shadow the moved one or keep serving the old release to the scoped update. It depends on `marketplace add` replacing an existing same-name declaration's source rather than refusing or ignoring it, which no one has observed (whether it does so is for the hands-on verification sibling to establish). It also moves a declaration no detected copy uses, such as a user-scope one that serves copies in other projects, and rewrites the tracked `.claude/settings.json` of a project whose copy stands only at another scope.

Mechanism: at each scope at which a Gurita copy applying to the open project was detected, the update runs `claude plugin marketplace remove gurita --scope <scope>`, then `claude plugin marketplace add --scope <scope>` with the new tag's source, then `claude plugin install gurita@gurita --scope <scope>`, so an update of Claude Code is a reinstall at each detected scope rather than a call to `claude plugin update`. Scopes moved: the detected copies' scopes only, since removing a declaration that serves copies elsewhere would take those copies with it; declarations at other scopes stay as they stand. It relies on no unobserved overwrite behaviour: removal and a fresh add are each the documented way to change a marketplace's source, so after the run each moved registration carries the new tag whatever `marketplace add` does to an existing name. Removing a marketplace may uninstall the plugins installed from it and drop their enabled state, so a failure between the removal and the reinstall leaves the harness with no Gurita copy at that scope; the update also stops being an update in Claude Code's own terms, and a disabled copy's state or its configuration may not survive the reinstall.

alternative.id: Rewrite ref at every declared scope

open-question.alternative: Mechanism: the extension itself rewrites the ref carried by the `gurita` marketplace declaration in the settings file of each scope where one applying to the open project stands (the user-scope marketplace record, the project's `.claude/settings.json`, the project's local settings), changing that field alone and running no marketplace add or remove. Scopes moved: every declared scope, whether or not a copy was detected there. Then `claude plugin marketplace update gurita` and the scoped `claude plugin update gurita@gurita -s <scope>` per detected scope, in the one run. The change is exactly one field per declaration, under the extension's own control and independent of how the CLI treats a repeated add, and no copy is uninstalled or left stale at any scope. It writes Claude Code's own settings and its internal marketplace record from outside the harness, against the goal's "by that harness's own install path", tying the extension to file formats Claude Code may change and that no CLI help documents, and it moves declarations no detected copy uses, the tracked `.claude/settings.json` included.

alternative.id: Rewrite ref at detected scopes only

open-question.alternative: Mechanism: the extension rewrites the ref field of the `gurita` marketplace declaration in the settings file of each scope at which a Gurita copy applying to the open project was detected, and of no other, running no marketplace add or remove; declarations at other scopes stay as they stand. Then `claude plugin marketplace update gurita` and the scoped `claude plugin update gurita@gurita -s <scope>` per detected scope, in the one run. It is the narrowest change: one field in each settings file paired with a copy being updated, with no reliance on the CLI's handling of a repeated add and no uninstall. It carries the same direct writes into Claude Code's own files, outside the harness's own install path, plus the risk that a same-name declaration left on the old tag at another scope is the one the scoped update resolves to.

open-question.question: Codex has no plugin update command, and `codex plugin marketplace upgrade` only refreshes the snapshot of the ref a marketplace was registered with, which for an install made from the Settings window is one release's tag. Which commands make up an update of the Codex Gurita copy to a newer release's tag?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: Removing and re-adding the registration leaves it at the new tag whatever `marketplace add` does to a name already configured, every command is one the CLI's help lists, and the update never uninstalls the plugin, so a failed step leaves the working copy in place rather than no copy at all.
open-question.alternative: The update moves the marketplace registration to the newer tag by removing it and adding it again, and then installs the plugin again over the copy still standing: `codex plugin marketplace remove gurita`, then `codex plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/gurita-codex --ref <tag>` (or `uHappyLogic/gurita-codex@<tag>`), then `codex plugin add gurita@gurita`, run in that order in one run, each behind the previous one's success. The installed plugin is never removed by the update itself. Every command is one the Codex CLI documents (`marketplace remove` and `add` with `--ref` both appear in its help text), the registration ends exactly as a fresh install from the window would leave it, at the newer tag, and the plugin is never deliberately uninstalled, so the copy stays in place if a later step fails. Whether `marketplace remove` leaves an installed plugin of that marketplace installed, orphaned, or uninstalled, and whether `plugin add` over an installed copy replaces it with the new version, is unobserved; a failure between the remove and the add leaves Codex with no `gurita` marketplace registered, and the old version's directory under `~/.codex/plugins/cache/gurita/gurita/` may stay behind beside the new one.

The update uninstalls the copy and its registration and installs both again at the newer tag: `codex plugin remove gurita@gurita`, then `codex plugin marketplace remove gurita`, then `codex plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/gurita-codex --ref <tag>`, then `codex plugin add gurita@gurita`, in that order in one run, each behind the previous one's success. It relies on no unobserved behaviour of a command run over existing state: every step acts on a known starting point, the old version's cache is removed by `plugin remove` as its help text states, and the end state is identical to a first install from the window. It is the longest sequence and the one that leaves Codex with no Gurita copy at all for the duration, so a failure after the first step (a network fault during `marketplace add`, for example) ends with the plugin uninstalled; it also discards whatever Codex recorded about the copy beyond its presence, such as its enabled state, and uses an uninstall command inside a window whose goal adds no uninstall control.

The update runs exactly the install's two commands again with the newer tag, removing nothing: `codex plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/gurita-codex --ref <tag>` over the already registered `gurita` marketplace, then `codex plugin add gurita@gurita`. Install and update share one command sequence and differ only in the tag read. It is the shortest sequence, one code path serves both Install and Update, and nothing is ever removed, so no failure can leave Codex with less than it had before the click. Whether `marketplace add` on a name already configured replaces its ref, refuses as a duplicate, or adds a second entry is unobserved and undocumented in the help text; if it refuses, the update cannot work at all, and if it silently keeps the old ref, the update reports success while the copy stays at the old release.

The update moves the marketplace registration to the newer tag by removing it and adding it again (`codex plugin marketplace remove gurita`, then `codex plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/gurita-codex --ref <tag>`) and runs no `codex plugin add`, leaving Codex to take the newer version from the refreshed marketplace snapshot for the copy already installed. It touches the installed plugin with no command at all, so the copy's install record and enabled state are never rewritten and the run is two commands. The installed copy stands in a version-keyed directory (`~/.codex/plugins/cache/gurita/gurita/<version>/`), which suggests that only an install writes a new version's files, so the update may end with the marketplace at the new tag and the plugin still at the old version; nothing observed so far shows Codex moving an installed copy to a newer snapshot by itself.

The update rewrites the ref of the `gurita` marketplace entry in `~/.codex/config.toml` to the newer tag, the extension writing that file itself, then runs `codex plugin marketplace upgrade gurita` to refresh the snapshot at the new ref and `codex plugin add gurita@gurita` to install the new version from it. It uses the one refresh command Codex offers for its intended purpose and changes nothing about the registration but its ref, with no window in which the marketplace is unregistered. The extension would write a configuration file Codex owns, whose layout for marketplace entries is neither documented in the CLI help nor stable across Codex releases, which departs from the goal's install by the harness's own install path and breaks silently when Codex changes that layout.

open-question.question: An install or update from the Settings window first reads the latest published release's tag from GitHub. When that read fails, for example with no network, an unreachable or rate-limited GitHub, or a distribution repository holding no release, what does the Install or Update that was clicked do?
open-question.recommendation: Every click then leads to a run and every failure to the one report path, with the cause printed in the terminal the person is already shown and the extension host still contacting no network, while each fallback would move a harness off the explicit release tag the published release ref decision requires or add stored state.
open-question.alternative: The lookup is not done by the extension. It is the first step of the script the install or update terminal runs, as the install run form decision describes. The script reads the tag, trying the API endpoint and then the page redirect. When both reads fail, it prints the cause in the terminal and exits with a non-zero status before any install, update, or marketplace command runs. The window then treats this like any other failed run. It reports the failure beside the harness or in a notification, and, because a run ended, it runs the whole harness check afresh as the check-after-install decision says. There is one failure path for everything that can go wrong in an install or update. The cause is visible in full in the terminal the person is already watching, and the extension host itself still makes no network call. A terminal opens and a harness check reruns for a run that never got started, which costs time (the check may take up to 120 seconds) and makes the cause less clear than a dedicated message. The lookup then depends on a network client being on the runner's shell, such as curl or python3's urllib, inside the session shell.

The extension reads the latest release's tag itself, through one read path (GitHub's releases/latest endpoint or the page redirect), before it opens any terminal. When that read fails, the clicked Install or Update stops there. No terminal is opened, no install, update, or marketplace command runs, and nothing on the harness changes. One VS Code error notification names the harness and the cause as the failure gave it: no network or GitHub unreachable, the rate limit, or no published release. There is no automatic retry and no action in the notification. Because no run ended, no fresh harness check runs and the kept result stands. The person clicks again later. It is the simplest and most predictable behaviour. Nothing is half-done, no harness is moved to a ref other than the one the published release ref decision names, and it uses the error notification the window already uses for a failed edit. Every failure, including a transient rate limit that a second request could get around, needs another click. A person working offline or behind a GitHub API limit cannot install from the window at all. It also adds the extension's first direct network call to an extension host that today contacts no network.

The extension reads the tag itself, before any terminal opens, first through GitHub's releases/latest API endpoint. If that read fails, it tries the /releases/latest page redirect once (or the other way round), with no further retry. Only when both reads fail does the Install or Update stop. From then on it behaves exactly as when it stops with a notification: no terminal, no command, nothing changed, one error notification naming the harness and the cause, and no fresh harness check. It covers the most likely non-offline failure. An unauthenticated API call is limited per hour per address, while the page redirect is not under that API limit, so a rate-limited lookup still finds the tag. It still never installs anything other than the latest published release. It means two lookup code paths to build and test, and two ways of reading the tag that must agree. It does nothing for no network or a repository with no release. A failure takes up to two round trips before it is reported.

The extension reads the tag itself before any terminal opens, through one read path. When the read fails, it runs nothing and shows an error notification naming the harness and the cause. The notification carries one action, for example "Install from main" or "Update from main". The action starts the same install or update against the distribution repository's `main` branch instead of a release tag. `main` is the branch the READMEs install from, and `/release-plugin` keeps it at the tagged commit. Dismissing the notification installs nothing. No harness check runs unless the action is taken and its run ends. A person blocked by a rate limit or a missing release can still install in one more click. Moving off the explicit tag is that person's own choice, never a silent substitution. The harness ends up tracking a branch rather than the tag the published release ref decision requires. Later updates and the version the window compares with then behave differently for that copy, and how an update moves a copy depends on how the Claude Code and Codex update steps are settled for a ref-less registration. It does nothing when there is no network, and it adds a second install form to build and test.

The extension reads the tag before any terminal opens. When the read fails for any reason, the clicked Install or Update runs anyway, at once, against the distribution repository's `main` branch: Antigravity's `archive/refs/heads/main.tar.gz`, and a Claude Code or Codex marketplace registered with no ref. The report of how the run ended adds one sentence saying the latest release could not be read and `main` was used. The harness check runs afresh when the run ends, as for any run. The click always does something whenever GitHub itself is reachable. It installs what the READMEs already document, and since `/release-plugin` keeps `main` at the latest tag, the files are normally the same as the release's. It silently drops the recorded explicit-tag ref in exactly the cases where the release is unknown. With no published release it installs unreleased `main`. A copy registered on `main` keeps following the branch on later updates, unlike tag-pinned copies. Every harness's update steps then need a second, ref-less form. With no network the fallback fails too, only later, inside the terminal.

The extension reads the tag before any terminal opens. When the read fails, the clicked Install or Update runs at once against the tag named by the version the extension was packaged from: `bundled/plugin_version.txt`, `2.0.0` today, passed as the explicit ref exactly as a latest tag would be. The report of how the run ended adds one sentence saying the latest release could not be read and the packaged version's release was used. The harness check runs afresh when the run ends. The ref stays an explicit, published release tag, as the published release ref decision requires. That tag is also the version the harness check compares with today, so the installed copy matches the packaged version the check reports against. The packaged version may be older than the latest release, so an Update can leave a copy unchanged or even move it backwards. The tag may not exist at all when the extension was packaged from an unreleased checkout, because the extension's own version and release are separate from the plugin's. With no network it fails anyway.

Every successful lookup stores the tag it read, per harness, in the per-user `~/.gurita/variants.json`, where the settings already live. When a later lookup fails, the clicked Install or Update runs at once against the stored tag as its explicit ref, and the report adds one sentence naming the tag used and saying the latest could not be read. When no tag is stored yet, it stops with an error notification naming the harness and the cause, runs nothing, and runs no harness check. A failed lookup still installs a release that was the latest one recently, always pinned to an explicit tag, so a brief rate limit or outage does not block a person who has looked up before. It adds new stored state to the settings file and a stale-value risk: the stored tag can be any age, and the window cannot tell how far behind it is. The very first lookup still fails with nothing to fall back on, and with no network the install fails anyway.

open-question.question: While an install or update started from the Settings window is still running in its terminal, which of the window's Install, Update, and Check again controls stay usable: can a second install or update be started, on the same harness or on another one, and can the harness check be run, before the first run ends?
open-question.recommendation: It is the one rule under which every check result shown after a run was taken after that run ended, since no second run or manual check can overlap it and swallow the check that follows, it needs a single running flag rather than a state per harness, and closing the run's terminal always releases a stuck run.
open-question.alternative: While any install or update run is going, every Install and Update control on every harness and scope and the Check again control are not usable until that run's terminal process ends, all drawn disabled, so at most one run goes at a time and no check runs beside it except the one that follows its end. The running note is kept in the extension's state for the session. The strongest guarantee: no two runs overlap and every check result the window shows after a run was taken after that run ended, extending the rule Check again already follows while a check runs to the whole Harnesses part. A run stuck at a prompt, on a slow download, or on a hanging CLI freezes the whole Harnesses part, re-check included, until it ends or its terminal is closed, and runs on different harnesses that would not interfere are serialized all the same.

The window tracks no install or update run for its controls: while a run is still going in its terminal, Install and Update stay usable on the same harness (every Claude Code scope included) and on the other harnesses, so any number of runs may go at once, and Check again stays usable too. Only the existing rule that Check again is disabled while a check runs still applies. Nothing new to hold or draw: the window keeps no note of running installs, the page gains no run state, and nothing a person might want to start is ever refused, which suits a run left waiting at a prompt in a terminal the person may not get back to soon. Two runs on the same harness can write the same files at once (Claude Code's settings and plugin records, the Antigravity directory extracted twice, the Codex marketplace configuration), and whether those CLIs tolerate that is unobserved. A Check again started during a run hides every Install and Update control while it runs, and if it is still running when the run ends, `checkHarnesses` returns early on its "unless one is running" guard, so the check after install is skipped and the kept result predates the run's end.

While a run on a harness is going, that harness's Install and Update controls (on Claude Code every scope's Install as well as Update) are not usable until the run's terminal process ends, drawn disabled as Check again is while a check runs; the other harnesses' Install and Update stay usable, so runs on different harnesses may go at once, and Check again stays usable. The note of which harness has a run is kept in the extension's state for the session, so a reopened window shows it. Blocks the one overlap most likely to break something, two runs writing the same harness's files, while still letting a person install or update all three harnesses side by side without waiting on each. With runs on two harnesses at once, the whole check that follows the first run's end runs while the second is still going and reports it mid-run, and a check still running when the second run ends swallows that run's own check through the same early-return guard, as a manual Check again during a run can; the window also gains a per-harness running state to hold and draw.

While a run on a harness is going, that harness's Install and Update controls are not usable until the run's terminal process ends, and Check again is not usable while any run is going; the other harnesses' Install and Update stay usable, so runs on different harnesses may go at once. Refused controls are drawn disabled, and the running note is kept in the extension's state for the session. Keeps side-by-side runs on different harnesses and the protection against same-harness collisions, while removing the manual check as a way to show a result from mid-run or to swallow the check that follows a run. A check after one run's end can still overlap another harness's run and swallow that run's own check when it ends during it, so the result can still predate a run's end; and the person cannot re-check at all while any run lasts, even one left waiting at a prompt.

Install and Update stay usable on every harness and every scope while a run is going, so any number of runs may go at once on the same harness or on others, and only Check again is not usable, drawn disabled, while any install or update run lasts. Guards only the check: a manual check can no longer show a result from mid-run or swallow the check after install, while no install or update is ever refused. Leaves same-harness runs free to write the same files at once, the overlap most likely to break an installation, and the overlapping checks that follow concurrent runs' ends can still skip one run's check; the person also cannot re-check during a long run.

While any install or update run is going, every Install and Update control on every harness and scope is not usable until that run's terminal process ends, drawn disabled, so at most one run goes at a time; Check again stays usable during the run. The running note is kept in the extension's state for the session. Mirrors the extension's existing one-run-per-mission rule for recipe runs (`ALREADY_RUNNING` in `src/runs.ts`) and rules out both same-harness collisions and overlapping post-run checks between runs, while the person can still re-check during a long run. Installing or updating all three harnesses becomes strictly sequential, and a run left waiting at a prompt or on a slow network blocks every other harness until it is answered or its terminal is closed; a Check again started during the run can still be running at its end and swallow the check after install.

open-question.question: The harness check counts an Antigravity or Codex Gurita copy that is installed but disabled as not installed. What does the Settings window offer for such a copy: Install, Update, or neither, saying instead that the copy must be enabled in the harness itself, as it does for a disabled Claude Code copy?
open-question.recommendation: It gives all three harnesses the rule already recorded for a disabled Claude Code copy, so the window never installs or updates over a state the person set on purpose and never reports a success that leaves the harness still reading as without a copy.
open-question.alternative: The harness check reports a disabled Antigravity or Codex copy as its own state, installed but disabled, beside the not-installed and installed states. For such a copy the window offers neither Install nor Update and adds no enable control; it says the copy is disabled and must be enabled in the harness itself, on Antigravity with `agy plugin enable gurita`, on Codex through its own plugin settings, matching what the window says for a disabled Claude Code copy. All three harnesses treat a disabled copy the same way, and the window never runs an install or update over a copy whose disabled state the person chose, so nothing it does can be mistaken for having fixed the copy or re-enable it behind the person's back. The check's print and its copy selection for both harnesses change, with their tests, and a disabled copy that is also out of date cannot be brought up to date from the window until it is enabled, an extra trip to the harness.

The harness check stays as it is: a disabled Antigravity `gurita` entry or a disabled Codex `gurita@gurita` entry is counted not installed, with no disabled state in the check's print. The Settings window treats such a harness exactly like one holding no copy, offering Install and no Update, and says nothing about the copy being disabled. Nothing in `harness_check.py`, its print, or the page's drawing changes, so the harness check and its tests stay exactly as the earlier mission left them and the window keeps one rule for every harness without a copy. Install runs over a copy that is already there: on Antigravity it extracts a release into the disabled copy's own directory, on Codex it re-adds a plugin already installed, and whether either leaves the copy disabled is unobserved, so the person can click Install, see it succeed, and still find the harness reporting no copy, with nothing on the page telling them why. How each command behaves over a disabled copy depends on how the mission observes the commands.

The harness check reports a disabled Antigravity or Codex copy as installed but disabled. The window offers Update for it, as for any installed copy, and no Install, and its line says the copy is disabled and must be enabled in the harness itself; no enable control is added. A disabled copy can still be brought to the latest release from the window, so it is current the moment the person enables it, and the line keeps the disabled state visible rather than hiding it as a missing copy. It departs from the disabled Claude Code rule, which offers nothing at a disabled scope, so the window treats a disabled copy two ways depending on the harness; and whether an update leaves an Antigravity or Codex copy disabled, or re-enables it, is unobserved and depends on how the mission observes the commands and on the update steps chosen for each harness.

The harness check reports a disabled Antigravity or Codex copy as installed but disabled, and the window offers neither Install nor Update for it. For Antigravity it adds one Enable control that runs `agy plugin enable gurita` in a terminal like an install, followed by the harness check afresh; for Codex, whose CLI has no enable command, it says the copy must be enabled in Codex itself. The commonest disabled case on a harness with an enable command is resolved with one click from the window, without the person having to know or type the harness's command. It adds a control the goal does not name and the disabled Claude Code decision declined for its own harness, makes the three harnesses differ in what a disabled copy offers, and has the window change a state the person set on purpose in the harness.
